description: Selected passages checked against the printed pages. This file is not a complete transcription of the Enchiridion.

chapters.text: Of Things, some are in our Power, and others not.
retained: Of Things, some are in our Power, and others not.

chapters.text:
Remember that Desire promises the Attainment of that of which you are desirous; and Aversion promises the Avoiding of that to which you are averse: that he who fails of the Object of his Desire, is disappointed: and he who incurs the Object of his Aversion, wretched.

Use only [the requisite Acts] of Pursuit and Avoidance; and even these lightly, and with Gentleness, and Reservation.
retained: Remember that Desire promises the Attainment of that of which you are desirous; and Aversion promises the Avoiding of that to which you are averse: that he who fails of the Object of his Desire, is disappointed: and he who incurs the Object of his Aversion, wretched.
Use only [the requisite Acts] of Pursuit and Avoidance; and even these lightly, and with Gentleness, and Reservation.

chapters.text: With regard to whatever Objects either delight the Mind, or contribute to Use, or are loved with fond Affection, remember to tell yourself, of what Nature they are, beginning from the most trifling Things.
retained: With regard to whatever Objects either delight the Mind, or contribute to Use, or are loved with fond Affection, remember to tell yourself, of what Nature they are, beginning from the most trifling Things.

chapters.text: When you are going about any Action, remind yourself of what Nature the Action is.
retained: When you are going about any Action, remind yourself of what Nature the Action is.

chapters.text: It is the Action of an uninstructed Person to lay the Fault of his own bad Condition upon others; of one entering upon Instruction, to lay the Fault on himself; and of one perfectly instructed, neither on others, nor on himself.
retained: It is the Action of an uninstructed Person to lay the Fault of his own bad Condition upon others; of one entering upon Instruction, to lay the Fault on himself; and of one perfectly instructed, neither on others, nor on himself.

chapters.text: Be not elated on any Excellence not your own.
retained: Be not elated on any Excellence not your own.

chapters.text: Thus likewise in Life, if, instead of an Onion, or a Shell-fish, such a Thing as a Wife or a Child be granted you, there is no Objection: but if the Captain calls, run to the Ship, leave all these Things, regard none of them.
retained: But if the Captain calls, run to the Ship, leave all these Things, regard none of them.

chapters.text: Require not Things to happen as you wish; but wish them to happen as they do happen; and you will go on well.
retained: Require not Things to happen as you wish; but wish them to happen as they do happen; and you will go on well.

chapters.text: For you will find it to be an Impediment to something else; but not to yourself.
retained: For you will find it to be an Impediment to something else; but not to yourself.

chapters.text: Upon every Accident, remember to turn towards yourself, and enquire, what Powers you have for making a proper Use of it.
retained: Upon every Accident, remember to turn towards yourself, and enquire, what Powers you have for making a proper Use of it.

chapters.text: Never say of any thing, "I have lost it;" but, "I have restored it."
retained: Never say of any thing, "I have lost it;" but, "I have restored it."

chapters.text: Begin therefore from little Things.
retained: Begin therefore from little Things.

chapters.text: If you would improve, be content to be thought foolish and stupid with regard to Externals.
retained: If you would improve, be content to be thought foolish and stupid with regard to Externals.

chapters.text: He is the Master of every other Person, who is able to confer, or remove, whatever that Person wishes either to have or to avoid.
retained: He is the Master of every other Person, who is able to confer, or remove, whatever that Person wishes either to have or to avoid.

chapters.text: Put out your Hand, and take your Share, with Moderation.
retained: Put out your Hand, and take your Share, with Moderation.

chapters.text: As far as Words go, however, do not disdain to condescend to him; and even, if it should so happen, to groan with him.
retained: As far as Words go, however, do not disdain to condescend to him; and even, if it should so happen, to groan with him.

chapters.text: Remember that you are an Actor in a Drama, of such a Kind as the Author pleases to make it.
retained: Remember that you are an Actor in a Drama, of such a Kind as the Author pleases to make it.

chapters.text: For which-ever of these Things happens, it is in my Power to derive Advantage from it.
retained: For whichever of these things happens, it is in your power to derive advantage from it.

chapters.text: You may be unconquerable, if you enter into no Combat, in which it is not in your own Power to conquer.
retained: You may be unconquerable, if you enter into no Combat, in which it is not in your own Power to conquer.

chapters.text: For, if you once gain Time and Respite, you will more easily command yourself.
retained: For, if you once gain Time and Respite, you will more easily command yourself.

chapters.text: Let Death and Exile, and all other Things which appear terrible, be daily before your Eyes; but chiefly Death: and you will never entertain any abject Thought, nor too eagerly covet any thing.
retained: Let Death and Exile, and all other Things which appear terrible, be daily before your Eyes; but chiefly Death: and you will never entertain any abject Thought, nor too eagerly covet any thing.

chapters.text: Now, for your Part, do not have a supercilious Look indeed; but keep steadily to those Things which appear best to you, as one appointed by God to this Station.
retained: Now, for your Part, do not have a supercilious Look indeed; but keep steadily to those Things which appear best to you, as one appointed by God to this Station.

chapters.text: Be contented then, in every thing, with being a Philosopher: and, if you wish to be thought so likewise by any one, appear so to yourself, and it will suffice you.
retained: Be contented then, in every thing, with being a tester: and, if you wish to be thought so likewise by any one, appear so to yourself, and it will suffice you.

chapters.text: Besides: which would you rather have a Sum of Money; or a Friend of Fidelity and Honour?
retained: Besides: which would you rather have a Sum of Money; or a Friend of Fidelity and Honour?

chapters.text: For as he hath the Lettuces, so you have the Half-penny, which you did not give.
retained: For as he hath the Lettuces, so you have the Half-penny, which you did not give.

chapters.text: Be assured then, that, when your own Cup likewise is broken, you ought to be affected just as when another's Cup was broken.
retained: Be assured then, that, when your own Cup likewise is broken, you ought to be affected just as when another's Cup was broken.

chapters.text: As a Mark is not set up for the Sake of missing the Aim, so neither doth the Nature of Evil exist in the World.
retained: As a Mark is not set up for the Sake of missing the Aim, so neither doth the Nature of Evil exist in the World.

chapters.text: And do you feel no Shame in delivering up your own Mind to be disconcerted, and confounded by any one, who happens to give you ill Language?
retained: And do you feel no Shame in delivering up your own Mind to be disconcerted, and confounded by any one, who happens to give you ill Language?

chapters.text: In every Affair consider what precedes and follows; and then undertake it.
retained: In every Affair consider what precedes and follows; and then undertake it.
chapters.location: Discourses III.15, referenced by Enchiridion XXIX

chapters.text: Duties are universally measured by Relations.
retained: Duties are universally measured by Relations.

chapters.text: For where Interest is, there too is Piety placed.
retained: For where Interest is, there too is Piety placed.

chapters.text: When, therefore, it is our Duty to share the Danger of a Friend, or of our Country, we ought not to consult the Oracle, whether we shall share it with them, or not.
retained: When, therefore, it is our Duty to share the Danger of a Friend, or of our Country, we ought not to consult the Oracle, whether we shall share it with them, or not.

chapters.text: Be for the most part silent: or speak merely what is necessary, and in few Words.
retained: Be for the most part silent: or speak merely what is necessary, and in few Words.

chapters.text: If you are struck by the Appearance of any promised Pleasure, guard yourself against being hurried away by it: but let the Affair wait your Leisure, and procure yourself some Delay.
retained: If you are struck by the Appearance of any promised Pleasure, guard yourself against being hurried away by it: but let the Affair wait your Leisure, and procure yourself some Delay.

chapters.text: When you do any thing from a clear Judgment that it ought to be done, never shun the being seen to do it, even though the World should make a wrong Supposition about it: for, if you do not act right, shun the Action itself; but, if you do, why are you afraid of those who censure you wrongly?
retained: When you do any thing from a clear Judgment that it ought to be done, never shun the being seen to do it, even though the World should make a wrong Supposition about it: for, if you do not act right, shun the Action itself; but, if you do, why are you afraid of those who censure you wrongly?

chapters.text: When you eat with another, then remember, not only the Value of those Things which are set before you, to the Body; but the Value of that Behaviour, which ought to be observed towards the Person who gives the Entertainment.
retained: When you eat with another, then remember, not only the Value of those Things which are set before you, to the Body; but the Value of that Behaviour, which ought to be observed towards the Person who gives the Entertainment.

chapters.text: If you have assumed any Character above your Strength, you have both made an ill Figure in that, and quitted one which you might have supported.
retained: If you have assumed any Character above your Strength, you have both made an ill Figure in that, and quitted one which you might have supported.

chapters.text: As, in walking, you take care not to tread upon a Nail, or turn your Foot; so likewise take care not to hurt the ruling Faculty of your Mind.
retained: As, in walking, you take care not to tread upon a Nail, or turn your Foot; so likewise take care not to hurt the ruling Faculty of your Mind.

chapters.text: The Body is to every one the measure of the Possessions proper for it; as the Foot is of the Shoe.
retained: The Body is to every one the measure of the Possessions proper for it; as the Foot is of the Shoe.

chapters.text: These should be done incidentally, and slightly; and our whole Attention be engaged in the Care of the Understanding.
retained: These should be done incidentally, and slightly; and our whole Attention be engaged in the Care of the Understanding.

chapters.text: It seemed so to him.
retained: It seemed so to him.

chapters.text: Every Thing hath two Handles; the one, by which it may be borne; the other, by which it cannot.
retained: Every Thing hath two Handles; the one, by which it may be borne; the other, by which it cannot.

chapters.text: These Reasonings are unconnected: "I am richer than you; therefore I am better:" "I am more eloquent than you; therefore I am better."
retained: These Reasonings are unconnected: "I am richer than you; therefore I am better:" "I am more eloquent than you; therefore I am better."

chapters.text: Do not say, that he doth it ill; but, in a mighty little time.
retained: Do not say, that he doth it ill; but, in a mighty little time.

chapters.text: For remember, that in this manner Socrates also universally avoided all Ostentation.
retained: For remember, that in this manner Socrates also universally avoided all Ostentation.

chapters.text: When you have brought yourself to supply the Necessities of your Body, at a small Price, do not pique yourself upon it: nor, if you drink Water, be saying upon every Occasion, "I drink Water."
retained: When you have brought yourself to supply the Necessities of your Body, at a small Price, do not pique yourself upon it: nor, if you drink Water, be saying upon every Occasion, "I drink Water."

chapters.text: But he goes about with the Caution of infirm People [after Sickness, or an Accident], dreading to move any thing that is set right, before it is perfectly fixed.
retained: But he goes about with the Caution of infirm People [after Sickness, or an Accident], dreading to move any thing that is set right, before it is perfectly fixed.

chapters.text: And when I find an Interpreter, what remains is, to make use of his Instructions.
retained: And when I find an Interpreter, what remains is, to make use of his Instructions.

chapters.text: And if any Instance of Pain, or Pleasure, or Glory, or Disgrace be set before you, remember, that now is the Combat, now the Olympiad comes on, nor can it be put off; and that, by once being worsted, and giving way, Proficiency is lost, or [by the contrary] preserved.
retained: And if any Instance of Pain, or Pleasure, or Glory, or Disgrace be set before you, remember, that now is the Combat, now the Olympiad comes on, nor can it be put off; and that, by once being worsted, and giving way, Proficiency is lost, or [by the contrary] preserved.

chapters.text: Therefore, at the same time that we lie, we are mighty ready to show how it is demonstrated, that Lying is not right.
retained: Therefore, at the same time that we lie, we are mighty ready to show how it is demonstrated, that Lying is not right.

chapters.text: Upon all Occasions, we ought to have these Maxims ready at hand.
retained: Upon all Occasions, we ought to have these Maxims ready at hand:
